[Poisson Regression]{.custom-title}




[Grayson White]{.custom-subtitle} [Stat 243
Fall 2026, Week 12]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Recall: GLMs A generalized linear model has three components: 1. A distribution of $y_i$ 2. A link function, $g(\mu_i)$, where $\mu_i = \mathbb{E}(y_i)$ 3. Linear predictor, $\eta_i$ ::: {.fragment} A GLM is written as follows: $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Dist(g^{-1}(\eta_i)) $$ where: ::: {.nonincremental} - $Dist$ is the assumed distribution of $y_i$, - $g^{-1}(\eta_i)$ is the value of the inverse link, which is $\mu_i$, and - $\eta_i$ is the linear predictor. ::: ::: ## Binary response GLMs **Logistic Regression:** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern\left(\frac{\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})}{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})}\right) $$ ::: {.nonincremental} 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Bernoulli 2. Link function: logit; $g(p_i) = \log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, so $p_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \frac{\exp(\eta_i)}{1 + \exp(\eta_i)}$ 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ::: ## Binary response GLMs ::: {.nonincremental} **Probit Regression:** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern(\Phi(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})) $$ 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Bernoulli 2. Link function: $g(p_i) = \Phi^{-1}(p_i)$, so $p_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \Phi(\eta_i)$, - where $\Phi(z)$ is the CDF of a standard normal random variable 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ::: ## Quantitative response GLM **Linear Regression:** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi},~ \sigma^2) $$ ::: {.nonincremental} 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Normal 2. Link function: identity; $g(\mu_i) = \mu_i$, so $\mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \eta_i$ 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ::: ## Count response GLM **Poisson Regression:** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Pois\left(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})\right) $$ ::: {.nonincremental} 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Poisson 2. Link function: log; $g(\lambda_i) = \log(\lambda_i)$, so $\lambda_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \exp(\eta_i)$ 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Recall: If $X \sim Pois(\lambda)$, then: - $\mathbb{E}(X) = \lambda$, and - $\mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda$. ::: ## A graphical comparison of Normal and Poisson regression ![](img/OLSpois-1.png){width='70%' fig-align='center'} ## Poisson regression assumptions Now that we have written down the Poisson regression model, $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Pois\left(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})\right) $$ we can see its assumptions: 1. **Poisson Response:** The response variable is a count, described by a Poisson distribution. 2. **Independence:** The observations must be independent of one another. 3. **Mean = Variance:** By definition, the mean of a Poisson random variable must be equal to its variance. 4. **Linearity:** The log of the mean rate, $\log(\lambda)$, must be a linear function of $x$. ## Poisson regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/proback/BeyondMLR/master/data/fHH1.csv") head(household) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 6 ...1 location age total numLT5 roof 1 1 CentralLuzon 65 0 0 Predominantly Strong Material 2 2 MetroManila 75 3 0 Predominantly Strong Material 3 3 DavaoRegion 54 4 0 Predominantly Strong Material 4 4 Visayas 49 3 0 Predominantly Strong Material 5 5 MetroManila 74 3 0 Predominantly Strong Material 6 6 Visayas 59 6 0 Predominantly Strong Material ``` ::: ::: - Data on households in the Philippines (more info: [Chapter 4.4 of Beyond MLR](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-BeyondMLR/ch-poissonreg.html)) - Each row represents a household - `age` = the age of the head of household - `total` = the number of people in the household other than the head ## Exploratory data analysis ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = household, mapping = aes(x = total)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Poisson regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_pois <- glm( formula = total ~ age, data = household, family = poisson(link = "log") ) broom::tidy(mod_pois) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 1.55 0.0503 30.8 1.07e-208 2 age -0.00471 0.000936 -5.03 5.01e- 7 ``` ::: ::: ## Plotting Poisson regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", method.args = list(family = poisson(link = "log"))) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Plotting Poisson vs linear regression ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", method.args = list(family = poisson(link = "log"))) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "tomato", linetype = "dashed") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: Linear regression produces nearly the same line. Advantages of Poisson regression? ## Poisson Assumptions: Have we met them? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_pois <- glm( formula = total ~ age, data = household, family = poisson(link = "log") ) broom::tidy(mod_pois) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 1.55 0.0503 30.8 1.07e-208 2 age -0.00471 0.000936 -5.03 5.01e- 7 ``` ::: ::: ## Poisson Assumptions **Poisson Response:** The response variable is a count, described by a Poisson distribution. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% ggplot(mapping = aes(x = total)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Poisson Assumptions **Poisson Response:** The response variable is a count, described by a Poisson distribution. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% mutate(age_bin = cut_width(age, width = 10)) %>% ggplot(mapping = aes(x = total)) + geom_bar() + facet_wrap(~age_bin, scales = "free") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Poisson Assumptions **Independence:** The observations must be independent of one another. - Check via data context. ## Poisson Assumptions **Mean = Variance:** By definition, the mean of a Poisson random variable must be equal to its variance. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% summarize(mean = mean(total), var = var(total)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 2 mean var 1 3.68 5.53 ``` ::: ::: - Note, this must be true across all "levels" of the predictor(s)! ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% mutate(age_bin = cut_width(age, width = 5)) %>% group_by(age_bin) %>% summarize(mean = mean(total), var = var(total), n = n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 17 × 4 age_bin mean var n 1 [17.5,22.5] 1.86 0.810 7 2 (22.5,27.5] 2.43 1.36 30 3 (27.5,32.5] 3 1.70 80 4 (32.5,37.5] 3.72 2.86 117 5 (37.5,42.5] 3.87 3.52 167 6 (42.5,47.5] 4.47 4.81 175 7 (47.5,52.5] 4.25 6.41 197 8 (52.5,57.5] 4.05 6.43 173 9 (57.5,62.5] 3.86 5.69 154 10 (62.5,67.5] 3.54 6.79 138 11 (67.5,72.5] 3.32 9.49 103 12 (72.5,77.5] 2.43 4.27 88 13 (77.5,82.5] 2.33 3.15 42 14 (82.5,87.5] 2 3 19 15 (87.5,92.5] 3.33 9.07 6 16 (92.5,97.5] 1.33 1.33 3 17 (97.5,102] 0 NA 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Poisson Assumptions **Linearity:** The log of the mean rate, $\log(\lambda)$, must be a linear function of $x$. ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% group_by(age) %>% summarize(empir_log_lambda = log(mean(total))) %>% ggplot(aes(x = age, y = empir_log_lambda)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: Plot of the log of **empirical** means against predictor levels. **Linear relationship??** ::: ## Poisson Assumptions Want to fix **linearity** and **Mean = Variance** assumptions. How? - **Linearity:** quadratic term will do the trick! - **Mean = Variance:** a bit harder... - However, this assumption only causes issues the value of our estimated standard errors (typically, these become under estimated), not our $\hat\beta$'s! - We can account for this degradation by estimating an **overdispersion** parameter! ## Overdispersion via quasi-Poisson In essence, an overdispersion parameter allows us to use the Poisson distribution to model counts through a GLM, when Mean $\neq$ Variance. For details on overdispersion, see [Beyond MLR Section 4.9](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-BeyondMLR/ch-poissonreg.html#sec-overdispPois). ::: {.fragment} In `R`, accounting for overdispersion and non-linearity: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_quasipois <- glm(total ~ poly(age, degree = 2), family = quasipoisson, data = household) summary(mod_quasipois) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = total ~ poly(age, degree = 2), family = quasipoisson, data = household) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 1.28739 0.01638 78.585 < 2e-16 *** poly(age, degree = 2)1 -3.35563 0.69839 -4.805 1.7e-06 *** poly(age, degree = 2)2 -6.83255 0.73837 -9.254 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for quasipoisson family taken to be 1.427994) Null deviance: 2362.5 on 1499 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 2200.9 on 1497 degrees of freedom AIC: NA Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Have an excellent break! See you Monday for linear mixed models.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
